standfirst: 1945 Gyeongseong, a pawnshop owner who can find anybody, a detective's daughter looking for her mother, and a hospital doing something in the basement. The history is the horror here, and the show is clear about it. These six keep the period, the creature or the confinement.

picks.why: A body used as a laboratory by an institution. Same premise of an organisation that knows exactly what it has made and keeps it filed, and the same use of creature horror to indict administration. Difference: it is contemporary, six episodes, and the emotional core is one isolated woman.

Occupation-era Korea taken seriously as a setting. Same period, same weight given to collaboration and resistance, same interest in who profits. Difference: no monster, no genre relief, and the pace is stately across twenty four hours.

A romance conducted while the country is being taken apart. Same balance of melodrama and history, with a lead who is flippant about everything except one person. Difference: it is a sageuk with no horror element and much better writing in its second half.

Ordinary bodies weaponised by people with offices. Both split their attention between a present-day search and what an older generation was forced to do. Difference: it is a superpower family saga with a 1990s spy half, and it is far more optimistic.

Historical setting, literal monster, romance intact. Same commitment to a creature with folklore behind it and a couple at the centre. Difference: it is a sageuk fantasy with comedy, so the dread never accumulates.

Period mystery about what a family buried. Same interest in an era's secrets and in an identity that does not check out. Difference: no creature and no institution, just one house and a very uncomfortable relationship.

against.title: Sweet Home
against.why: The reflex creature-horror pick. It is a contemporary siege in an apartment block with monsters as metaphor for despair, and none of the colonial history that makes this specific.

against.title: Kingdom
against.why: Named as the historical horror standard. It is a political thriller with zombies and an excellent script; Gyeongseong Creature is a romance with a monster and a much softer spine.

against.title: Squid Game
against.why: Recommended because it is the Netflix Korean default. There is no game, no allegory and no ensemble here, and the villain is a documented occupying force.
